# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |

| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |

"""Estimate the elastic modulus of each material from linear fits to
stress-strain data.

For each specimen, stress is regressed on strain with ordinary least squares
(slope + intercept); the slope is the elastic modulus. Material values are
reported as the mean and standard deviation of the specimen moduli, alongside a
pooled fit across all specimens of that material.
"""

import os

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA_PATH = "measurements.csv"
RESULTS_PATH = "results/moduli.csv"
SPECIMEN_RESULTS_PATH = "results/specimen-moduli.csv"
FIG_PATH = "figures/stress-strain.png"

# Fixed material order and colors (first three categorical slots, validated
# all-pairs for scatter plots), with distinct markers as secondary encoding
MATERIALS = ["steel", "titanium", "aluminum"]
COLORS = {"steel": "#2a78d6", "titanium": "#eb6834", "aluminum": "#1baf7a"}
MARKERS = {"steel": "o", "titanium": "s", "aluminum": "^"}


def linear_fit(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    """Fit y = slope * x + intercept and return the fit statistics."""
    (slope, intercept), cov = np.polyfit(x, y, deg=1, cov=True)
    y_pred = slope * x + intercept
    ss_res = np.sum((y - y_pred) ** 2)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
    return {
        "slope": slope,
        "slope_se": np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]),
        "intercept": intercept,
        "r_squared": 1 - ss_res / ss_tot,
    }


df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)

# Per-specimen fits
specimen_rows = []
for (material, specimen), g in df.groupby(["material", "specimen"]):
    fit = linear_fit(g["strain"].values, g["stress_mpa"].values)
    specimen_rows.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "specimen": specimen,
            "n_points": len(g),
            "modulus_gpa": fit["slope"] / 1e3,
            "modulus_se_gpa": fit["slope_se"] / 1e3,
            "intercept_mpa": fit["intercept"],
            "r_squared": fit["r_squared"],
        }
    )
specimens = pd.DataFrame(specimen_rows)

# Per-material summary
material_rows = []
pooled_fits = {}
for material in MATERIALS:
    g = df[df["material"] == material]
    s = specimens[specimens["material"] == material]
    pooled = linear_fit(g["strain"].values, g["stress_mpa"].values)
    pooled_fits[material] = pooled
    material_rows.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "n_specimens": len(s),
            "modulus_mean_gpa": s["modulus_gpa"].mean(),
            "modulus_std_gpa": s["modulus_gpa"].std(ddof=1),
            "modulus_cv_pct": 100
            * s["modulus_gpa"].std(ddof=1)
            / s["modulus_gpa"].mean(),
            "pooled_modulus_gpa": pooled["slope"] / 1e3,
            "pooled_modulus_se_gpa": pooled["slope_se"] / 1e3,
            "pooled_intercept_mpa": pooled["intercept"],
            "pooled_r_squared": pooled["r_squared"],
        }
    )
summary = pd.DataFrame(material_rows)

os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(RESULTS_PATH), exist_ok=True)
specimens.round(6).to_csv(SPECIMEN_RESULTS_PATH, index=False)
summary.round(6).to_csv(RESULTS_PATH, index=False)
print(summary.round(3).to_string(index=False))

# Figure: data points by material with pooled linear fits
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5), layout="constrained")
strain_line = np.linspace(0, df["strain"].max() * 1.02, 50)
for material in MATERIALS:
    g = df[df["material"] == material]
    fit = pooled_fits[material]
    color = COLORS[material]
    ax.plot(
        g["strain"] * 100,
        g["stress_mpa"],
        linestyle="none",
        marker=MARKERS[material],
        markersize=6,
        markerfacecolor=color,
        markeredgecolor="white",
        markeredgewidth=0.8,
        alpha=0.85,
        label=f"{material.capitalize()} (data)",
    )
    ax.plot(
        strain_line * 100,
        fit["slope"] * strain_line + fit["intercept"],
        color=color,
        linewidth=2,
    )
    # Direct label at the end of each fit line
    x_end = strain_line[-1]
    ax.annotate(
        f"{material.capitalize()}: E = {fit['slope'] / 1e3:.0f} GPa",
        xy=(x_end * 100, fit["slope"] * x_end + fit["intercept"]),
        xytext=(6, 0),
        textcoords="offset points",
        va="center",
        fontsize=9,
        color="#0b0b0b",
    )
ax.set_xlabel("Strain (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress (MPa)")
ax.set_xlim(0, df["strain"].max() * 100 * 1.02)
ax.set_ylim(0, None)
ax.grid(True, color="#e4e3df", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for side in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
for side in ["left", "bottom"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_color("#8a8984")
ax.tick_params(colors="#52514e")
ax.legend(title="Lines: pooled linear fits", frameon=False, loc="upper left")
# Leave room on the right for the direct labels
ax.set_xlim(right=df["strain"].max() * 100 * 1.45)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(0, df["strain"].max() * 100 * 1.02)

os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(FIG_PATH), exist_ok=True)
fig.savefig(FIG_PATH, dpi=200)

# Elastic modulus from tensile test data

## Data

Tensile test measurements (`measurements.csv`) were taken for three specimens
each of steel, titanium, and aluminum. Each specimen has 10 stress readings at
strains from 0.02% to 0.20%, all within the linear-elastic region.

## Method

For each specimen, stress was regressed on strain with an ordinary
least-squares linear fit (slope and intercept). The slope is the elastic
(Young's) modulus, $$E$$. Each material's modulus is reported as the mean and
sample standard deviation of its three specimen values. A pooled fit over all
points for each material was also computed. Because every specimen was
measured at the same strains, the pooled slope equals the mean of the specimen
slopes exactly. The standard error of the pooled slope reflects scatter about
the line, not variation between specimens.

## Results

| Material | Specimens | $$E$$ (GPa), mean ± SD | CV (%) | Pooled fit $$R^2$$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
$summary_table

Per-specimen fits:

| Specimen | Material | $$E$$ (GPa) | Std. error (GPa) | Intercept (MPa) | $$R^2$$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
$specimen_table

![Stress vs. strain with pooled linear fits](figures/stress-strain.png)

## Discussion

- Every specimen is very close to linear ($$R^2 \geq$$ $min_r2), so a linear fit
  suits this strain range. The fitted intercepts are all within
  $max_abs_intercept MPa of zero, which suggests no meaningful offset or toe
  region in the data.
- Specimen-to-specimen variation is small: the coefficient of variation is at
  most $max_cv% for any material.
- Steel is about $steel_al_ratio times stiffer than aluminum, and titanium about
  $ti_al_ratio times stiffer. The estimates match typical handbook values
  (steel ≈ 200 GPa, titanium alloys ≈ 105–120 GPa, aluminum alloys ≈ 69 GPa).
- Caveat: there are only three specimens per material, so the standard
  deviations are themselves uncertain. A 95% confidence interval on each mean
  is about ±2.5 SD.

*This report is generated by the `write-report` stage of the Calkit pipeline
from `report-template.md` and `results/`; edit the template, not this file.*

"""Fill the report template with values from the fit results."""

from string import Template

import pandas as pd

TEMPLATE_PATH = "report-template.md"
REPORT_PATH = "report.md"

summary = pd.read_csv("results/moduli.csv").set_index("material")
specimens = pd.read_csv("results/specimen-moduli.csv")

summary_table = "\n".join(
    f"| {m.capitalize()} | {r.n_specimens} "
    f"| {r.modulus_mean_gpa:.1f} ± {r.modulus_std_gpa:.1f} "
    f"| {r.modulus_cv_pct:.1f} | {r.pooled_r_squared:.4f} |"
    for m, r in summary.iterrows()
)
specimen_table = "\n".join(
    f"| {r.specimen} | {r.material} | {r.modulus_gpa:.1f} "
    f"| {r.modulus_se_gpa:.2f} | {r.intercept_mpa:.2f} | {r.r_squared:.4f} |"
    for r in specimens.sort_values("specimen").itertuples()
)
e = summary["modulus_mean_gpa"]

with open(TEMPLATE_PATH) as f:
    template = Template(f.read())

report = template.substitute(
    summary_table=summary_table,
    specimen_table=specimen_table,
    min_r2=f"{specimens['r_squared'].min():.4f}",
    max_abs_intercept=f"{specimens['intercept_mpa'].abs().max():.1f}",
    max_cv=f"{summary['modulus_cv_pct'].max():.1f}",
    steel_al_ratio=f"{e['steel'] / e['aluminum']:.1f}",
    ti_al_ratio=f"{e['titanium'] / e['aluminum']:.1f}",

# Elastic modulus from tensile test data

## Data

Tensile test measurements (`measurements.csv`) were taken for three specimens
each of steel, titanium, and aluminum. Each specimen has 10 stress readings at
strains from 0.02% to 0.20%, all within the linear-elastic region.

## Method

For each specimen, stress was regressed on strain with an ordinary
least-squares linear fit (slope and intercept). The slope is the elastic
(Young's) modulus, $E$. Each material's modulus is reported as the mean and
sample standard deviation of its three specimen values. A pooled fit over all
points for each material was also computed. Because every specimen was
measured at the same strains, the pooled slope equals the mean of the specimen
slopes exactly. The standard error of the pooled slope reflects scatter about
the line, not variation between specimens.

## Results

| Material | Specimens | $E$ (GPa), mean ± SD | CV (%) | Pooled fit $R^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steel | 3.0 | 199.1 ± 2.0 | 1.0 | 0.9984 |
| Titanium | 3.0 | 116.6 ± 1.7 | 1.5 | 0.9979 |
| Aluminum | 3.0 | 69.4 ± 1.8 | 2.5 | 0.9983 |

Per-specimen fits:

| Specimen | Material | $E$ (GPa) | Std. error (GPa) | Intercept (MPa) | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| TI-2 | titanium | 117.8 | 1.64 | -2.22 | 0.9985 |
| TI-3 | titanium | 117.2 | 1.50 | -0.08 | 0.9987 |

## Discussion
